design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of proportions (PROSPERO CRD42019133166) estimating the prevalence and risk of cannabis use disorder (CUD), cannabis abuse (CA) and cannabis dependence (CD), by DSM or ICD criteria from structured interviews, among people in general-population samples who had used cannabis. Cohorts were sought in PubMed and cross-sectional surveys in the Global Burden of Disease data input sources (studies published from January 2009; searched February 2019, updated April 2020); 21 studies gave 153 data points. Subgroups by design and by recall period of use (lifetime, past year or month, weekly or daily); meta-regression on year of data collection, tool and country adjusted for age, sex and recall period. Read from the journal pre-proof (accepted manuscript).
can_establish: The average share of people who had used cannabis who met DSM criteria for cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence in general-population studies from high-income countries published 2009 to 2020, and how it differed by design and by how often people had used.
cannot_establish: The risk for any one product, form or strength (no included study estimated risk by potency), the risk outside high-income countries, or a precise lifetime risk of developing a disorder, because lifetime, past-year and past-month measures are pooled together and the included studies were not appraised.

sample.recruitment: PubMed (MeSH 'marijuana abuse' AND 'cohort studies', with title and abstract synonyms) for longitudinal studies and the Global Burden of Disease data input sources for cross-sectional studies, searched in February 2019 for papers from January 2009; supplemented by reference lists, key population surveys, drug monitoring agency publications, references forwarded by experts, the authors' collection and a search for new publications in April 2020 (Method › Search strategy, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Observational general-population studies reporting DSM or ICD cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence ascertained by structured clinical interviews; high-risk or sub-populations such as prisoners or ethnic minorities excluded, as were unvalidated scales, self-reported problems and studies published before 2009 (Method › Selection criteria; Search strategy, pp. 5-6). Full texts excluded: 9 not observational general-population studies, 48 without data on the disorders, 31 without estimates among people who had used cannabis, 21 duplicating data in another included study (Results › Study selection, p. 8).
sample.demographics: Samples from the US (over half of the studies), the Netherlands, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and France; 11 studies sampled adolescents or young adults, one older adults and the rest broad age ranges such as 12 or older or 18 or older (Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 1st paragraph, p. 8; Discussion, 12th paragraph, p. 15). Table 1 gives no sample size for any study.
sample.attrition: Not reported for the included cohorts.
sample.selection_effects: General-population surveys from high-income countries only. Definitions of a person who uses cannabis range from having tried it once to daily use: nine studies counted people who had ever tried cannabis, three required more than a few occasions, nine past-year use and four weekly or daily use (Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 2nd paragraph, p. 8). Excluding studies published before 2009 leaves out the early-1990s survey behind the widely cited one-in-ten dependence figure, which the review discusses separately (Introduction, p. 4).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported cannabis use in each survey, recorded as ever used, number of times used, past-year, past-month, or weekly or daily use (Method › Data extraction, p. 7).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency only through these recall categories; no data on potency, form or route. The authors found no population study that estimated cannabis use disorder risk by the potency of products used (Discussion, 11th paragraph, p. 15).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; other substance use disorders are named only as a topic for future research (Discussion, 14th paragraph, p. 16).

comparison.controls: None; proportions among people who had used cannabis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a pooled prevalence; age and sex differences and age of first use are summarised from the studies that reported them.

outcomes.instruments: Structured diagnostic interviews: CIDI and M-CIDI, AUDADIS-IV and AUDADIS-5, SCID and DIGS, and DSM-IV criteria-based tools in the US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (Table 1). One study used DSM-III-R and one DSM-5; the rest used DSM-IV, in which cannabis use disorder means abuse or dependence (Discussion, 13th paragraph, p. 16).
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of the included studies is reported. A Canadian study using the Severity of Dependence Scale was excluded for not using a structured interview; it classed 10.5% of adolescents who used cannabis in the past year as dependent (p. 16).
outcomes.operationalization: Prevalence over the lifetime, the past 3 years, the past year or the past month, or incidence at follow-up, of cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence among people who had used cannabis as each study defined use; several data points per study by sex, age, survey year or recall period (Method › Data extraction, p. 7; Table 1 footnote).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable; three outcome pools, each with subgroups and a meta-regression.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled proportions with 95% CI (Table 2, p. 28). Cannabis use disorder: overall 0.22 (0.18 to 0.26); longitudinal, lifetime use 0.27 (0.25 to 0.28), recent use 0.22 (0.20 to 0.24); cross-sectional, lifetime 0.28 (0.10 to 0.48), recent 0.17 (0.12 to 0.23), regular (weekly or daily) 0.22 (0.17 to 0.28). Abuse: overall 0.13 (0.08 to 0.18); longitudinal recent 0.17 (0.14 to 0.20); cross-sectional lifetime 0.20 (0.14 to 0.26), recent 0.10 (0.03 to 0.19), regular 0.08 (0.02 to 0.16). Dependence: overall 0.13 (0.10 to 0.15); longitudinal lifetime 0.12 (0.07 to 0.18), recent 0.09 (0.01 to 0.19), regular 0.33 (0.22 to 0.44); cross-sectional lifetime 0.11 (0.07 to 0.15), recent 0.08 (0.06 to 0.10), regular 0.18 (0.12 to 0.24). Q, I2 and the studies in each pool are in S4 (not read). Meta-regression: year of data collection moderated cannabis use disorder (B = -0.01, p = 0.049) and abuse (B = -0.01, p = 0.017), not dependence (B = 0.00, p = 0.270); age, sex, recall period, assessment tool and country did not (p. 12).
analysis.covariates: Meta-regression adjusted for study-level age, sex and recall period.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42019133166, described as an a priori protocol; PRISMA checklist in S1 (p. 5). Separate analyses for each DSM version were planned (Method › Selection criteria, 2nd paragraph, p. 6) but are not reported, and the main pools combine DSM-III-R, DSM-IV and DSM-5 estimates. The registry record was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Heterogeneity statistics, forest plots and the studies in each pool are only in the supplement; Table 1 gives no sample sizes; the abstract and conclusions report the overall pools and the cohort figure for regular use, not the lower cross-sectional figure for daily use.
analysis.power: The authors state they had limited power to detect moderators other than year of data collection (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 14).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 21 general-population studies from high-income countries (153 data points), the pooled share of people who had used cannabis who met criteria was 22% (18 to 26) for cannabis use disorder, 13% (8 to 18) for abuse and 13% (10 to 15) for dependence. Single-study estimates of use disorder ranged from 4.5% (US adults aged 50 or more) to 41.1% (Australian 21-year-olds), and of dependence from 3.5% (young adults in Ireland) to 40.9% (daily use in an Australian adolescent cohort). Dependence was 33% (22 to 44) in two longitudinal studies of young people who used weekly or daily, and 18% (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use. No study estimated risk by potency.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions present the pooled shares as risks (1 in 5 for use disorder, 1 in 8 for abuse or dependence) and extend the cohort figure to people who use cannabis weekly or more often (1 in 3); the Discussion says closer to 1 in 8 people who have used cannabis will develop dependence and that clinicians "can have confidence in using this updated figure". Gaps: (1) the pools mix lifetime, past-3-year, past-year and past-month prevalence with incidence, so they are not a lifetime risk of developing a disorder, as the authors themselves caution (Discussion, 9th paragraph); (2) the 1 in 3 figure comes from two cohorts of young people in Australia and the Netherlands, while cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use gave 18%; (3) confidence is claimed without heterogeneity statistics in the main text and without any appraisal of the pooled studies; (4) the abstract's message on early initiation does not mention that two of four studies found no association with dependence; (5) the Introduction and Conclusions point to more potent products, but no study in the review measured potency. Against this, the Discussion names the heterogeneity, the reliance on cross-sectional surveys, the different recall periods, the high-income samples and the lack of potency data.

timeline.event: US National Comorbidity Survey (1990-92): 9.1% of people who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), the one-in-ten figure this review sets out to update
US NESARC analysis of transition from first use to dependence, one of the 21 included studies; the encyclopedia's card of it gives a lifetime cumulative probability of 8.9% for cannabis
This review: by its authors' account, the first meta-analysis of epidemiological studies of the prevalence and risk of cannabis use disorder among people who use cannabis.
Systematic review of cannabis potency and mental ill health and addiction, which cites this review's 22% in its Introduction

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent pooled general-population figures read for the encyclopedia: about 22 in 100 people who had used cannabis met criteria for a use disorder and about 13 in 100 for dependence, in high-income countries, mostly by DSM-IV. They update the older one-in-ten figure but pool recall periods and DSM versions without appraising the studies; the stratified figures (lifetime, recent, regular use; cohort or survey) are more informative for a base rate than the overall pool. No figure is available by potency or form. The NESARC estimate in Table 1 should be checked against the primary paper (see reporting issues).

The funding bodies had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Role of Funding Sources, pp. 28-29).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest (Conflict of Interest, p. 29).

what_would_settle_it: Repeated general-population cohorts that record when people start using cannabis, how often they use it, which products and how much THC, and that measure DSM-5 cannabis use disorder by interview over time, reporting cumulative incidence by frequency, product strength and form, in high-income and low- and middle-income countries.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people in general-population samples who had used cannabis), outcomes (DSM or ICD cannabis use disorder, abuse and dependence from structured interviews) and designs (observational) are stated; a prevalence question needs no comparator (Method › Selection criteria, p. 5).

PROSPERO CRD42019133166, described as an a priori protocol, with a PRISMA checklist in S1 (p. 5). The registry record was not read; separate analyses by DSM version were planned (p. 6) but are not reported, and the change is not explained.
Cross-sectional surveys were included alongside cohorts because there were too few cohorts, with the consequence discussed (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 14).

PubMed for cohorts (MeSH terms named, full terms in S3a, not read) and the Global Burden of Disease data input sources for cross-sectional surveys, supplemented by reference lists, key population surveys, drug monitoring agency publications, references from experts, the authors' collection and an update in April 2020 (p. 6). The restriction to studies published from 2009 is explained by the aim; language limits are not stated; only one bibliographic database was searched, with a narrow strategy for cohorts.
Who screened titles, abstracts and full texts is not stated, and no duplicate screening is reported (Method › Study selection, p. 6).
Who extracted the data is not stated beyond the contributors' roles (two authors acquired and analysed the data); no duplicate extraction is reported (pp. 7, 29).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for the 109 full-text exclusions are counted in the text (9, 48, 31 and 21; p. 8); the flowchart is in S1 and examples of excluded studies in S3c, which were not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, study name, years and design, ages, the definition of use, the outcome definition, the diagnostic tool, the percentage and sex and age differences, but no sample size or response rate for any study (pp. 24-27).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No assessment of the risk of bias or quality of the included studies is reported.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of proportions, but several data points per study (by sex, age, survey year or recall period) were extracted as separate data points (p. 7) with no stated handling of their dependence, the method for pooling proportions is not stated, and the overall pools combine lifetime, past-year and past-month prevalence with incidence; forest plots are in S4 (not read). Judged from the main text.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the impact of risk of bias, which was not assessed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Without an appraisal of the included studies, the interpretation could not account for their risk of bias; the Discussion considers recall bias in cross-sectional surveys and stratifies by design (p. 14), which concerns designs, not the studies pooled.

Subgroups by design and recall period and meta-regression on year of data collection, assessment tool and country (adjusted for age, sex and recall period) investigated heterogeneity, and the Discussion names it as a limitation (pp. 11-12, 14); I2 values are only in S4.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the authors' conflicts are declared (pp. 28-29).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from supplements S1 and S3c, which were not read. Four critical items fail (9, no appraisal of the included studies; 11, several dependent data points per study pooled across recall periods without stated handling; 13; 15), so confidence is critically low whatever item 7 shows. This is a judgment on how far the pooled percentages can be trusted as a precise summary, not on the usefulness of the review: it is registered, restricted to structured diagnostic interviews in general-population samples, stratifies by design and recall period, and its stratified figures broadly agree (about 17 to 28 in 100 for use disorder, about 8 to 12 in 100 for dependence among people who had used, higher with regular use). Cite it for the order of size and the spread, with the recall periods and populations named; take single-study figures from the primary papers where possible.

key_findings.finding: 1,383 records identified, 1,264 unique titles screened, 130 full texts assessed, 109 excluded (9 not observational general-population studies, 48 without data on the disorders, 31 without estimates among people who had used cannabis, 21 duplicating data), leaving 21 studies with 153 data points and 255,010, 28,951 and 58,661 observations for cannabis use disorder, abuse and dependence.

Samples from the US, the Netherlands, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and France; 15 studies gave cross-sectional and 9 longitudinal data; 11 sampled adolescents or young adults and one older adults. Nine studies counted people who had ever tried cannabis, three required use more than a few times, nine past-year use and four weekly or daily use; three cohorts reported incidence in people without a disorder at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: One study used DSM-5 (lifetime probability of transition to cannabis use disorder after use 27%), one DSM-III-R (26.4%, 20.9 to 32.0, given lifetime use), the rest DSM-IV (for example 23.7%, 19.7 to 27.7, in a Dutch cohort). In a US survey that approximated DSM-5 with DSM-IV-based criteria, 16.8% (15.9 to 17.7) of adults who had used cannabis in the past year, and 36.8% (34.4 to 39.3) of those who used it daily or near daily, met two or more criteria.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Single-study extremes: cannabis use disorder from 4.5% (1.8 to 7.3) in US adults aged 50 or more who used in the past year (2005-06) to 41.1% (38.4 to 43.8), lifetime, in an Australian cohort of 21-year-olds; abuse from 2.9% (2.5 to 3.3) in US adults in 2017 to 28.4% (25.8 to 30.9) in a 2001-02 US survey; dependence from 3.5% (0.1 to 7.0) in young adults in Ireland to 40.9% (29.0 to 52.8) among people using daily in an Australian adolescent cohort (22.6%, 15.2 to 29.9, with weekly use); past-year dependence 14.7% (13.0 to 16.5) among US adults using daily or near daily in 2017.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 4th to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Most of the ten studies that reported sex differences found higher risk in males; US studies consistently found higher risk at younger ages. Earlier first use went with higher risk of use disorder and abuse in the studies that examined it, while for dependence two studies found higher risk with earlier use and two did not.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Pooled shares: cannabis use disorder 22% (18 to 26); longitudinal lifetime 27% (25 to 28) and recent 22% (20 to 24); cross-sectional lifetime 28% (10 to 48), past year 17% (12 to 23), daily or near daily 22% (17 to 28). Abuse 13% (8 to 18). Dependence 13% (10 to 15); longitudinal lifetime 12% (7 to 18) and recent 9% (1 to 19); cross-sectional lifetime 11% (7 to 15) and recent 8% (6 to 10); weekly or daily use 33% (22 to 44) in cohorts and 18% (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 11); Table 2 (p. 28)

key_findings.finding: Year of data collection moderated the pooled prevalence of cannabis use disorder (B = -0.01, p = 0.049) and abuse (B = -0.01, p = 0.017) but not dependence (B = 0.00, p = 0.270), an effect the authors attribute to lower prevalence over time in the one US survey reported across years; age, sex, recall period, tool and country did not moderate the estimates.

The Discussion says the 13% for dependence is slightly higher than the one-in-ten figure, that closer to 1 in 8 people who have used cannabis will develop dependence, and that clinicians, researchers and policymakers can have confidence in the updated figure. The 33% for weekly or daily use comes from two cohorts of young people (Australia and the Netherlands); cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use gave 18% (12 to 24). In one US study, dependence was 10.6% (7.1 to 14.1) among everyone who had ever used and 18.1% (12.4 to 23.8) among those who had used more than six times.

Limitations stated: heterogeneity, with estimates possibly too different to pool and limited power to detect moderators; 60% of estimates from cross-sectional surveys open to recall bias; past-year and lifetime estimates that mean different things (past-year use disorder 15.4% among 18 to 25-year-olds who used that year against 9.8% among those who had ever used, in one US survey).

No population study estimated the risk of cannabis use disorder by the potency of the cannabis used; the authors mention, without a reference, a Michigan study of high-risk families in which people who used higher-potency products had higher risks of developing use-disorder symptoms. All included studies were from high-income countries and over half from the US.

Conclusions: people who use cannabis have a 1 in 5 risk of a use disorder (abuse or dependence) and a 1 in 8 risk of abuse or dependence, rising to 1 in 3 for dependence among people who use weekly or more often; these risks may rise if people use more often and use more potent products after legalisation.

Funding: University of Queensland development fellowship (JL); NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship (LH); Australian Government Drug and Alcohol Program funding of the authors' centre and group; funders had no role. All authors declare no conflicts of interest.
key_findings.locator: Role of Funding Sources; Contributors; Conflict of Interest

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the same odds ratio and interval, 2.20 (1.37 to 3.52), for two different variables in a study of older adults: the number of joints smoked at peak use and the frequency of use.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is probably a copying error; neither can be used without the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: A Michigan study of high-risk families, said to show higher risks of use-disorder symptoms with higher-potency products, is described without any reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The only potency finding in the review cannot be traced from it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels the NESARC-III analysis of 2012-13 (Feingold 2020) longitudinal and the analysis of the same survey wave by Hasin (2015) cross-sectional. The only Table 1 rows labelled longitudinal that give lifetime use disorder are Feingold (27.0%), Kirisci (26.4%) and Prince van Leeuwen (23.7%), so the longitudinal lifetime pool of 27% (25 to 28) appears to rest on them (editors' reading; the studies in each pool are listed only in S4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The longitudinal lifetime figure for use disorder may rest largely on a single-wave survey; quote it with that caution.

reporting_issues.issue: For the NESARC cohort (Lopez-Quintero 2011), Table 1 gives 7.2% (6.6 to 7.7) 'past year' dependence among people who had ever used cannabis, and the text says 70% of people with lifetime dependence started before 14. The encyclopedia's card of that paper (sc_lopez_quintero_2011, read in full by another reader) gives a lifetime cumulative probability of dependence of 8.9% for cannabis, does not list 7.2%, and records that onset before 14 predicted cannabis dependence only before adjustment, reversing after it (hazard ratio 0.63).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's figure for this study and its use of it for early onset need checking against the primary paper; the base rate should not lean on this row.

reporting_issues.issue: Separate analyses for each DSM version were planned but are not reported, and the pools combine DSM-III-R, DSM-IV and DSM-5 estimates; Table 1 gives no sample size for any study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The weight of each study in a pool cannot be judged from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: A review article about one cohort (Coffey & Patton 2016, on the Victorian Adolescent Health Cohort Study) is an included data source, although the selection criteria say reviews were used only to find references; and the Introduction's description of the 2007 Australian survey is garbled (risk if people had used cannabis five times or in their lives).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the cohort's figures come second-hand through that review.
